articles.title: Trade Centre UK: Newlyweds among dozens in dispute with dealer
articles.summary: Thirty-four customers battling for refunds on faulty cars as Trading Standards investigates.
articles.body:
Newlyweds Amber and Nathan Cooper spent all their wedding present money on a £7,000 Citroen C4 to take them on their dream honeymoon.

But as they made their way to Cornwall in August 2025, it lost power and began to roll backwards leaving them stranded on the A30, near the Jamaica Inn in Bodmin Moor, they told the BBC.

When they returned it to Trade Centre UK two weeks later, they discovered it needed a new engine, clutch and gearbox.

But a year on, they are still fighting for an apology and their money back.

They are among 34 customers who told the BBC that they also bought cars from Trade Centre UK branches in Coventry, Rochdale, Rotherham and Wales but are still locked in a battle for refunds.

Customers say they have been left with loud noises from the engine, suspension and clutch problems. The company insists problems are "rare".

They have said that when they rejected the vehicle under the Consumer Rights Act, the process through Trade Centre UK was complicated, lengthy and their claims were often refused.

Amber said: "It's gutted us mentally, emotionally, physically, financially, I don't know what we can do apart from get this story out and have people learn from our mistake."

Trade Centre UK has said it takes concerns raised "very seriously" and recognises that "problems can sometimes occur".

A statement from the company said: "On these rare occasions, our teams work with customers to investigate the issue and identify an appropriate resolution, which can include repairs, replacement vehicles or, where appropriate, accepting rejection of a vehicle."

The couple from Wolverhampton said they have been left in debt and emotional turmoil as they spent a year having to hire and borrow cars before taking out a loan to replace what they lost.

Amber added: "People are coming to us and asking are you enjoying your wedding present?

"We have to say, 'No, it's sitting in the Trade Centre's car park'. We're having to apologise to people who turned up to our wedding and kindly gave us money.

"My husband works in Telford, which is a 60-mile round trip every day, and without a car he has had to miss work which means we've lost even more money.

"We're still in debt, trying to pay off this loan and now I can't save for a house, start a family and move on with my life."

Connor and Danielle Johnson-Bray from Stoke-on-Trent also bought their car from the Wednesbury branch last September.

They say it broke down within two days, so they were offered a different one, which subsequently broke down three times in eight months.

Connor explained: "We spent £2,200 on repairs, courtesy cars, and just the initial getting the car, trying to get it back on the road."

After being refused a refund, they took their case to the small claims court against the finance company they had bought the car through, who agreed to settle.

Danielle added: "We did accept that [settlement], and it meant that we did lose a lot of money as well. We didn't have any more fight left in us.

"It had drained us, we were very stressed, we were tired, I wasn't sleeping."

As part of a BBC Investigation in July , Michelle Chancellor, from Stourport-on-Severn, Worcestershire, shared that she bought her Vauxhall from the Wednesbury branch of The Trade Centre UK but soon heard loud noises coming from the engine.

After appearing in BBC coverage she was contacted by the used car dealer, who told her that the refund was accepted.

She said: "It was another two to three weeks until my refund came through and I was able to buy a new car, which meant I was still losing out on income after signing the rejection papers.

"I think that the financial loss will affect me for a while yet, especially as I'm a self-employed mature student that lives alone."

Sandwell Council Trading Standards has confirmed it has launched an investigation into the complaints and has urged anyone with issues to report concerns via the Citizens Advice Consumer Service.

Consumer expert Stuart Masson explained that it is worrying when multiple customers feel they have no option but to pursue disputes because they believe a dealership is failing to cooperate.

"It's enormously frustrating, the Consumer Rights Act has to be fair to both parties when it comes to buying used cars," he said.

"It should be easy, especially within the first month. After six months it becomes more complicated. But it sounds like a lot of these problems are happening within the first few weeks."

Trade Centre UK's statement added: "We are committed to meeting our responsibilities to our customers and continue to invest in our vehicle preparation, aftersales and customer service operations.

"We are proud to have been in operation across the UK for over 20 years and to have served hundreds of thousands of customers during that time."

articles.title: Coroner asks families linked to jailed surgeon to make contact
articles.summary: Surgeon Ian Paterson is serving a 20-year sentence for his botched and unnecessary operations.
articles.body:
A coroner investigating the deaths of people treated by the jailed breast surgeon Ian Paterson has appealed for 106 more patients' families to make contact.

Inquests are currently being heard into the deaths of 70 women, to see if Paterson's treatment or care caused an unnatural death.

Paterson was jailed in 2017 after being convicted of wounding patients by way of botched and unnecessary operations and given a 20-year prison sentence.

The inquests' coroner, Judge Richard Foster, said he was recently notified of the deaths of a further 106 patients who were in their lifetime treated by Paterson for breast cancer, but he said he had not been told of their medical cause of death.

The list of 106 names, including six men, appears on the investigation website asking next of kin to contact the solicitors to the inquests Higgs LLP.

The law firm told the BBC: "We are simply seeking cause of death information to assess whether the deaths of these former patients of Mr Paterson will be investigated."

The disgraced breast surgeon worked with cancer patients at NHS and private hospitals in the West Midlands over 14 years.

At his trial the court heard that Paterson's technique involved leaving some breast tissue behind, preserving patients' cleavages, which breached national guidelines.

Investigations have so far found 106 patients died between 1995 and July 2026.

Others had surgery they did not need - some even finding out years later they did not have cancer.

The surgeries caused serious lasting physical and physiological harm to all the victims. One woman was unable to breast feed her baby as a result.

Paterson is due to be automatically released halfway through his sentence in 2027, before the inquests in Birmingham are due to conclude.

articles.title: London designer turns waste mussel shells and local Thames sand into glass; wins £10,000 Design Museum prize
articles.summary: London designer Lulu Harrison has won the 2025 Ralph Saltzman Prize from the Design Museum for Thames Glass, a project that turns locally sourced and
articles.body: London designer Lulu Harrison has won the 2025 Ralph Saltzman Prize from the Design Museum for Thames Glass, a project that turns locally sourced and waste materials into glass. Harrison's recipes use materials including sand from around the River Thames, wood ash and waste quagga mussel shells supplied by Thames Water. The Design Museum describes Harrison as a geo-alchemist glass artist whose project explores the possibility of creating geo-specific glass from abundant and waste materials associated with a particular place. Harrison was selected as the fourth recipient of the annual prize by a jury comprising industrial designer Konstantin Grcic, material designer Seetal Solanki, artist and designer Stephen Burks and design journalist and author Michelle Ogundehin, alongside Lisa Saltzman. The judges praised Harrison's research and her approach to mapping the raw materials used in the glass and communicating that process to audiences. She received a £10,000 bursary to continue developing her work.Quagga mussel shells became one of the key ingredientsA central component of Thames Glass is the shell of the quagga mussel, an invasive non-native species that can cause blockages in Thames Water's transfer tunnels and has to be removed. Harrison says her collaboration with Thames Water gave her access to the waste shells, which would otherwise require disposal. She combines ground-up mussel shells with local sand and waste wood ash to create different glass recipes. Her own project description says the work began with experiments using local and waste materials sourced in and around the Thames, including waste shells from water companies and wood ash or bracken from surrounding forests. The resulting glass has been used to create objects including carafes, tumblers and other vessels, with the material's natural impurities contributing to its distinctive appearance. Harrison developed the project while studying for an MA in Material Futures at Central Saint Martins and has worked with glassblowers, glass chemists and glass archaeologists during its development.Thames Glass grew from a collaboration with Thames WaterThe project developed through Harrison's work with Thames Water while she was studying at Central Saint Martins. Harrison has said that the collaboration helped her find a use for the tonnes of quagga mussel shells being removed because the animals were blocking water infrastructure. Her early work produced prototypes of a Thames Glass carafe and tumbler, while later experiments explored other forms and applications. Central Saint Martins documented the project in 2022, describing Harrison's use of local sands, waste shells and wood ash and her collaboration with Thames Water. Harrison has also worked with Here Design, glassblowers and other specialists to develop the material and its applications. Rather than presenting Thames Glass as a replacement for conventional glass, Harrison describes the project as an exploration of alternative glassmaking recipes based on materials associated with a particular geographical area.The material has also been tested as architectural claddingHarrison later worked with London architecture studio Bureau de Change to investigate whether Thames Glass could be used on buildings. The collaboration produced a series of cast glass façade tiles made using the material, with patterns inspired by London's architectural history, including designs found on 19th-century terracotta chimney pots. The tiles were presented as part of Beautility: How Fusing Beauty and Function Can Change the World, an exhibition curated by Here Design during London Craft Week. Bureau de Change says the project explored whether Thames Glass could be used as an alternative material for building cladding, while Harrison's own project page describes the tiles as an exploration of future applications for the material. The collaboration therefore moved Thames Glass beyond vessels and into architectural experimentation, although the work remains a design and material research project rather than an established commercial building product.The prize will support Harrison's next stage of researchThe Ralph Saltzman Prize gives Harrison £10,000 to continue developing Thames Glass and provides an opportunity to display the project at the Design Museum. The museum describes the prize as an annual award for emerging product designers whose practices explore new directions in design, including technical innovation, sustainability and cultural re-evaluation. Harrison's 2025 project was displayed at the museum from June 24 to August 25, 2025. In describing the award, Harrison said her practice is driven by research, process, collaboration, experimentation and hands-on making, connecting craft and science while exploring more localised possibilities for glassmaking. Thames Glass is still fundamentally an experimental material project, but its use of waste quagga mussel shells, local sand and waste ash demonstrates how materials removed from one system can become ingredients in another.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Ask India, Pakistan, Bangladesh': Nepal PM Balen Shah flags broken world order at UNGA
articles.summary: Nepal prime Minister Balendra Shah on Thursday warned the United Nations General Assembly about the devastating impact of climate change.
articles.body: Nepal prime Minister Balendra Shah on Thursday warned the United Nations General Assembly about the devastating impact of climate change. He said catastrophic floods that killed at least 1,400 people in the country highlighted the human cost of a crisis borne most severely by those least responsible for it.Addressing the UN General Assembly, Shah said the crisis was not limited to Nepal and pointed to the wider impact of climate change and conflict across South Asia."We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food. And this is not Nepal’s private misfortune. Ask Bangladesh, ask Bhutan, ask India, ask the Maldives, ask Pakistan, ask Sri Lanka, ask any other country in our region and you’ll hear the same account."Shah said Nepal and other countries in the region were facing the consequences of crises they had not caused."Hit by the climate we did not warm and again hit by the wars we did not start," said Balen Shah.More than 6,000 people remain missing, while the damage is estimated at around 10 per cent of Nepal’s gross domestic product (GDP).“The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world,” he said. “And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?”Shah said the warming climate was destabilising the Himalayan ecosystem, with melting permafrost making mountain slopes increasingly unstable and raising the risk of avalanches, floods and landslides.He added that the devastation extended across Nepal’s border with China and downstream into India.“Climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped on passports," Shah said.The floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 5,130 people remain missing, while 13,728 people have been rescued so far. Only 104 bodies have been identified and handed over to their families. Meanwhile, 339 people are undergoing treatment in 19 hospitals, while 3,761 displaced people are staying in 37 holding centres.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Bangkok roads submerged as flood disaster declared
articles.summary: An emergency has been declared across the capital of Thailand as days of heavy rain leave the city inundated.
articles.body:
A flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok after 48 hours of heavy rain left roads in the Thai capital submerged.

People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors.

Thunderstorms are common in Thailand at this time of year but extreme weather in recent days has inundated Bangkok's drainage system, causing traffic chaos on roads that are already famously congested.

The rain is expected to continue into Sunday, raising fears that more canals could burst their banks.

Somkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, told the AFP news agency: "The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now.

"I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now."

She said water levels in the city appeared to be worse than in 2011, when Bangkok was impacted by nationwide flooding.

Hundreds were killed across Thailand then in an extreme weather event that lasted for three months. So far, no casualties have been reported in Bangkok from this latest flooding.

The Thai Meteorological Service has forecast more heavy rain through the week, though the area of low pressure causing the downpours of recent days is expected to move towards central Thailand.

All 50 of Bangkok's districts have been declared emergency zones.

Chadchart Sittipunt, the city's governor, said the east of the city had been hardest hit, AFP reported.

He continued: "The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full... The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled."

articles.title: Bradford's 'hidden gem' Pictureville Cinema hosts 30th film festival
articles.summary: Pictureville Cinema showcases film across a range of formats, including 70mm, 35mm and Cinerama.
articles.body:
A Bradford cinema that offers screenings in a "unique" format is celebrating 30 years of its film festival.

Pictureville Cinema, based at the National Science and Media Museum, hosts its Widescreen Weekend each year, showcasing films in a range of formats, including 70mm, 35mm and Cinerama.

Cinerama technology, developed in the 1950s, uses three synchronised projectors to display images onto a deeply curved wide screen.

Jack Weedon, Screen Programme Producer for the festival, said: "We are kind of a hidden gem, because it is kind of a niche interest, so it kind of flies under people's radar."

Widescreen Weekend was first held in 1996 and only included six films.

Organisers said Pictureville was the last remaining place in the world to watch Cinerama following the closure of two other specialised cinemas in 2020.

"It is fantastic to see because a lot of cultural events are kind of plateauing or they are maybe dying off, especially with the increasing costs for running things like this.

"We have got people here from Australia, Poland, America, Canada, we've got France, we've got the Netherlands, Germany, and they come every year just for this and it is really, really great for the region."

One of the main attractions of the festival is the ability to showcase Cinerama.

"This requires three cameras to film it, three projectors to project it, and three projectionists working all together at once to create this huge, wide and curved image," said Weedon.

This year's programme includes a newly loaned print of 1962 film How the West Was Won, and a restored 70mm print of 1977 sci-fi classic Close Encounters of the Third Kind.

Other highlights include an Imax screening of Interstellar and a showing of Jurassic Park 3D.

"What we do here is we celebrate unique film experiences," said Weedon.

"It is so unique because we have lots of different ways that you can see film here and people are getting more and more familiar with them these days."

Weedon said the peak in public interest around cinema technology was likely a byproduct of the success of Sir Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey and the interest in the Imax format.

"Some of the best filmmakers around - Paul Thomas Anderson, Quentin Tarantino and Christopher Nolan - their passion projects are working with these increasingly rare technologies and they're reviving formats that have long since died.

"It is kind of being propelled by these people who are very influential in cinema."

Nolan's take on Homer's epic poem, which was released earlier this year, took $264m (£198m) at cinema box offices globally in its opening weekend, including $52m (£39m) on giant Imax screens.

articles.title: Disaster zone declared across Bangkok as heavy rain triggers flooding
articles.summary: Nonstop rain since Thursday has submerged Thai capital’s roads and canals, sending water into homes and stores.
articles.body:
Bangkok authorities have declared a disaster zone across all 50 districts of Thailand’s capital after three consecutive days of rainfall caused heavy flooding.

The disaster designation, which gives local organisations authority to take action, came on Saturday after Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said almost 300mm (11.8 inches) of rain had fallen since Thursday afternoon.

The nonstop rain inundated roads and canals with water, sending water into many homes and stores alongside them, according to reports. Photos and videos showed major roads submerged and cars abandoned after drivers were unable to move through the rising water.

Chadchart said the east of the city was most impacted and warned that more rain was forecast again on Saturday. He added that flooding should recede once the rain subsides, as city officials work to drain floodwaters as quickly as possible.

“The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full,” he said on social media. “The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled.”

Later on Saturday, the government said the flooding situation had “stabilised” but added it would still take two or three days for the water to drain, as long as the rain held off. “If more rainwater doesn’t fall in the area, it will be solved,” he said.

Chadchart also advised residents to move their cars to higher ground, as Bangkok’s public transport authority offered free access to MRT train “park and ride” carparks to store their vehicles until October 2.

Reporting from a flooded street in Bangkok, Al Jazeera’s Tony Cheng said the Thai capital is no stranger to heavy rain during the monsoon season, but the continuous rainfall had locals worried.

“What usually happens is we get heavy downpours for a couple of hours, then you’ll see the street often flooded but it would flow away into the drains quickly, and it would only happen in isolated areas too,” he said.

“What’s happening here is … happening all across the city. This is not a flash flood; this is persistent heavy rain since Thursday evening, and it shows no sign of letting up.”

Somkid Pheuk-ngam, 67, a vendor who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, said she had to close her shop for two days.

“The water keeps coming in. It’s hard to go out now. It’s at my waist level,” she told the AFP news agency. “I cannot go anywhere,” she said, adding that this was “worse than the 2011 flood.”

Widespread flooding across Thailand in 2011 killed more than 500 people and damaged millions of homes.

The Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation has warned of low pressure across eastern, northeastern and central Thailand until Sunday, saying there was a risk of flash floods, forest runoff, mudslides and river overflow.

articles.title: In 2011, Philadelphia began a $2 billion plan to turn hard blocks into rain gardens and porous streets; by 2021 it kept an estimated 3.08 billion gallons of stormwater out of waterways each year
articles.summary: Discover how Philadelphia's innovative Green City, Clean Waters program cut sewer overflows by 3.08 billion gallons annually, reshaping urban water management through eco-friendly solutions like rain gardens and porous streets.
articles.body: Philadelphia is one of the oldest cities in America, and for decades its water-absorbing streets, rooftops, and sidewalks were progressively covered with hard surfaces, until the pipe networks beneath them could no longer handle the runoff. The city struggled with this for many years before taking an environmentally focused approach to resolving a grave infrastructural issue.A city built above underground streamsSome 60 percent of Philadelphia uses what engineers call a combined sewer system, in which rainwater and domestic sewage flow together through the same pipes to treatment plants. That system works in dry weather, but heavy rain can overwhelm the pipes, sending a mix of stormwater and untreated sewage into rivers and streams. For a community between the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers, this meant billions of gallons of filthy water finding its way into local waterways every single year.By the early 2000s, the problem was too big to ignore, and Philadelphia officials began searching for an alternative to the standard solution of creating huge underground storage caverns and tunnels, an approach estimated to cost the city as much as nine billion dollars. Eventually, the Environmental Protection Agency approved a totally different strategy, one centred on softening the city rather than merely burying more concrete beneath it.A twenty-five-year bet on green infrastructureIn 2011, Philadelphia began Green City, Clean Waters, a twenty-five-year programme with an investment of approximately $2.4 billion. It was structured on rain gardens, tree trenches, porous pavement and vegetated planters that were designed to soak up stormwater before it ever reaches a sewer line. Rain was no longer seen as waste to be drained away as quickly as possible but as a resource to be captured, slowed down and allowed to seep organically into the ground. Streets that had poured every drop of rain directly into the sewer system were repaved with materials that allowed water to seep through, and empty lots and schoolyards were recontoured into little basins that could catch storm runoff.Since the initiative began, the Philadelphia Water Department has supervised the roll-out of more than a thousand of these green stormwater projects city-wide, spread throughout parks, sidewalks, transit corridors and private properties. A decade into the plan, by 2021, the Philadelphia Water Department reported that this network of small-scale interventions was keeping an estimated 3.08 billion gallons of polluted stormwater out of the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers every year, a volume that would otherwise have poured straight into the city's waterways during heavy rain.The individual components of this system are intentionally tiny and unglamorous, and that is part of why the total achievement is easy to miss. One rain garden may only collect a small amount of water from one block, one porous parking lot may soak up runoff from one storm and one row of street trees may slow rain on its way down. But multiplied across thousands of such sites across the city, the cumulative impact is that a significant portion of Philadelphia’s overall stormwater burden is being handled before it ever gets to an outdated pipe network.A model that other cities are eyeing onPhiladelphia's approach has gained attention far beyond its borders, and NACTO has profiled it as one of the largest green street projects at city scale, noting that the programme has deployed green infrastructure across more than 28,000 acres of the city's combined sewer area. Part of the attraction is the economics. It has generally been cheaper to build green infrastructure over thousands of smaller sites than to build a few enormous subterranean tunnels and it has ancillary benefits no concrete tunnel ever could, from shaded streets and reduced summer heat to slightly higher property prices in the communities where the work has been done.And none of this indicates the initiative has outright solved Philadelphia's stormwater problem. Rainfall patterns have intensified since the plan was first drawn up in 2009, and the city may eventually need to combine its green strategy with more grey infrastructure to keep up with larger storms. But even so, the core assumption underlying Green City, Clean Waters, that a city can make a real reduction in sewage pollution by rethinking its streets, not just its pipes, has already changed how planners in other flood-prone areas think about stormwater.Delegations from other cities often visit Philadelphia to learn how the programme was conceived, financed and implemented on this scale, and numerous towns have subsequently drafted their versions of green stormwater plans, taking Philadelphia’s approach as the starting template. Whatever the city ultimately does to adapt to the increased rainfall, the core premise that redesigning streets and vacant lots can compensate for the massive subsurface infrastructure has shown that street redesign can help reduce pressure on subsurface infrastructure, one rain garden and permeable pavement at a time.You use AI every day. articles.title: India takes next step to develop the next generation of space age rail guns
articles.summary: India has taken a fresh step towards building an indigenous electromagnetic launcher capability, with Heavy Vehicles Factory, Avadi floating expressions
articles.body: India has taken a fresh step towards building an indigenous electromagnetic launcher capability, with Heavy Vehicles Factory, Avadi floating expressions of interest for the design, development and supply of key components of an Electromagnetic Launcher, or EML, system. The move signals that the country is now looking to move the technology beyond laboratory research and into industrial-scale development.The first expression of interest, issued by Armoured Vehicles Nigam Limited, seeks an industry partner for the design, development and supply of an EM launch barrel assembly along with electrical accessories. A second notice issued the very next day seeks partners for the barrel's platform and drives. While the final weapon configuration and performance requirements have not been disclosed, the two tenders together point towards simultaneous work on the launcher, its electrical systems and its mechanical mounting.An electromagnetic railgun works fundamentally differently from conventional artillery, using electrical energy rather than chemical propellants to fire a projectile. A high-current pulse passed through two conducting rails and a moving armature generates the electromagnetic force needed to accelerate the projectile down the barrel at extremely high speed, well beyond what conventional guns can achieve. The DRDO has been developing this capability around high-power energy systems, specialised rails, protective coatings, switching devices and targeting systems.The scale of ambition is significant. DRDO's programme has envisaged a 100-megajoule railgun capable of firing an 18-kg projectile at speeds exceeding 2,000 metres per second, as reported by Jane's. For reference the highest velocity tank round can only reach speeds of up to 1,780 metres per second. Potential calibres up to 155 mm and ranges between 100 and 400 km, though these remain development goals rather than proven capabilities. The technology is being explored for naval strike roles, anti-ship warfare and air defence, given its potential to reduce flight time and simplify ammunition storage. The US has taken steps to operationalise these guns on naval platforms.The challenges to operationalise this system are substantial, chief among these challenges are generating and delivering such enormous electrical energy in a short pulse demands high-capacity capacitor banks and advanced switching technology. Barrel and rail wear from extreme electrical and thermal stress is another major hurdle, which is why DRDO is focusing on friction-reduction coatings and erosion-resistant materials, alongside recoil systems and high-mobility vehicle mounting, which are to be developed by the Armament Research and Development Establishment (ARDE). Learnings from this project can also be used in the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS), which can be used to launch fixed wing aircraft from aircraft carriers.India joins a small group of nations, which includes the US, China, Japan, Turkey, France and Germany, that are publicly known to be pursuing military railgun technology at various stages. For India, the expression of interest marks a meaningful shift from laboratory demonstration towards industrial partnership, though the real test will lie in overcoming the power, durability and repeat-fire challenges needed to turn the technology into an operationally deployable weapon.

articles.title: China, US to open AI ‘communication channel’ after summit, White House says
articles.summary: White House says the two countries agreed to open a ‘bilateral communication channel’ for AI incidents.
articles.body:
The United States and China have agreed to establish a “communication channel” for artificial intelligence (AI) incidents, the White House said after a summit in Washington, DC.

US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping discussed matters ranging from AI and trade to the stalled war in Iran during a three-day state visit, and confirmed that they would meet for a third and fourth time this year at international summits in China and the US.

The White House said on Friday that the nations agreed to establish a “bilateral communication channel” for AI incidents. There was no immediate comment from Beijing on the White House statement.

The announcement came after a summit short on breakthroughs that was dominated by ceremony, according to Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher, reporting from the White House.

“There was a lot of ceremony and a lot of pomp. In fact, there was a lot more pomp than progress,” Fisher said. The two sides agreed to extend a trade truce due to expire in November, pushing the deadline to January “to give both sides the chance to talk”.

Trump said the visit had strengthened his personal rapport with Xi, which he said would benefit the US in the long run.

“We’ve had a tremendous visit from two spectacular people, and we really enjoyed it, and I think we’ve made tremendous strides,” Trump said. “We’ve made great strides, very positive for both countries.”

Calling on both nations to pursue “a healthy competition” that acts as “a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses”, President Xi stated that as “leading nations in artificial intelligence”, the two powers share “the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good”.

Fisher reported that Xi used the summit to press specific aims, seeking assurance that China would be “treated more fairly” in future dealings and laying out guidelines he wants to shape upcoming talks between the two countries.

Xinhua reported Xi also urged Trump to “handle the Taiwan issue prudently” along with discussions on the Middle East, Ukraine, and the Korean Peninsula.

On trade, the White House said China agreed to import at least 10 million metric tonnes of US coal in 2027-2028, with more favourable tariffs on $30bn of “non-sensitive goods” each way. Two pandas are also set to arrive at a US zoo.

The visit featured a state banquet, a military parade and a tour of the National Archives, where the leaders viewed the Declaration of Independence and Constitution. Trump noted the US “goes 250 years; theirs goes 6,000 years”.

The two leaders will meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December.

Fisher said the continuation of dialogue was “perhaps the biggest deliverable for both sides”.

articles.title: Memorial for pupils given contaminated blood at Treloar's
articles.summary: During the 1970s and 1980s pupils received medical treatments using contaminated blood products.
articles.body:
A memorial has been created at a school where boys were experimented on and infected with HIV and hepatitis.

During the 1970s and 1980s, the Lord Mayor Treloar School and College in Hampshire offered specialist care for children with haemophilia but pupils received medical treatments using contaminated blood products .

Of the 122 pupils with haemophilia that attended the school, only about 30 were still alive when the Infected Blood Public Inquiry published its report into the scandal in 2024.

It highlighted how "very few" of the pupils with haemophilia that attended the school between 1970 and 1987 "escaped being infected".

It said children were treated as "objects for research" and were experimented on without their knowledge by NHS clinicians, who knew the dangers it posed.

The memorial installed at the college, near Alton, Hampshire, depicts two pupils, one with a sling and and another holding a cane, embracing each other.

Adrian Goodyear, 55, who first attended Treloar's when he was nine, said: "We couldn't believe the place we were looking at. Rolling country hills, swimming pools, canoes, a Jacobian mansion. It was just remarkable at first.

Goodyear was infected with hepatitis and HIV while at the school.

"In 1985, a doctor tearfully said that I had two to three years to live," he explained.

"I was told this with five other boys and the doctor went round the room and said: 'You have… you haven't… you have… you haven't… you have got HIV'."

He said the memorial was important to keep the scandal "in the public consciousness" and to honour those who died.

He added: "When we were here we made promises… they died in front of us, one winter we lost five boys.

"I made promises to them, as did the other lads here today, that we would never give up. We would find out what happened."

If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

Gary Webster, 61, who was infected with HIV and hepatitis C when he attended between 1975 and 1983, was called to the doctor's office one dinnertime as a child, and told he had two years to live.

He said that the memorial was important "to remember what happened and to make sure it never happens again".

Steve Nicholls, 59, who attended the school from 1976 to 1983, said the memorial "represents me 50 years ago, it represents the boys 50 years ago, it's what we were".

"It resembles the comradeship and the bonds that were formed at the college at the time," he continued.

"I have known the majority of these boys for 50 years. I went to school with them for eight years. We played together, we slept in the same dormitories as each other and we were treated together. So, we became like brothers.

"We were often referred to as blood brothers and we've stayed in contact throughout the years.

He added: "We feel incredibly guilty for surviving it and getting through it when many of our friends didn't."

Richard Warwick, who attended the school between 1976 and 1982, said the memorial was a "symbol of comradeship, friendship and support".

The inquiry found that medical research was carried out at Treloar's "to an extent which appears unparalleled elsewhere".

In his report Sir Brian Langstaff said it had "left long scars, not only in this Hampshire community but across the UK".

Des Collins, senior partner of Collins Solicitors, said: "Today is about remembering the real-life consequences of responsibilities, at a local and state level."

Reading a statement on the trust's behalf at the time, Toby Riley-Smith KC said it was "so sorry" that many former pupils were among the affected.

"It is so sorry that as a result, they and their loved ones have suffered so much, and for so long.

"It is so sorry that they have been victims of this tragedy, which Sir Brian Langstaff has described as the worst treatment disaster in the history of the NHS, a tragedy that has been compounded by the fact that it has taken so long for their plight to be recognised."

More than £2bn has now been paid in compensation to victims across the UK of the infected blood scandal .

articles.title: Angela Rayner criticises worker visa plans on eve of Labour conference
articles.summary: The housing secretary says the government's plans to change wait times for permanent residency are unfair because they "change the goalposts".
articles.body:
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said she is concerned about Labour's proposals to change visa rules, which would make it harder for foreign workers to secure permanent residency in the UK.

In an interview with the Times ahead of Labour's annual conference, Rayner questioned Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's plans, saying they are unfair because they "change the goalposts".

Under the proposals, most migrants would have to wait 10 years to qualify for residency - instead of the current five - while foreign workers on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait.

Mahmood said the government would make a decision on the immigration overhaul by the end of the year.

Speaking to the Times, Rayner said she was concerned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules.

She described the potential rule change as "very disruptive" and added: "I do have concerns about that."

During her interview with the Times, she said that the changes would impact foreign care workers who "moved their lives here to look after our loved ones".

Her remarks represent direct criticism of a policy inherited by Prime Minister Andy Burnham from his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.

Rayner previously served as deputy prime minister under Sir Keir, and was brought back into cabinet by Burnham in July.

It is significant that a serving cabinet minister feels able to criticise an existing government proposal on the eve of Labour's conference, albeit one inherited from the Starmer era.

It is part of a growing head of steam from some parts of the party to quash the retrospective elements of these plans.

Rayner has previously criticised the measures. In June, she said proposals to retrospectively alter the rules for migrants already working in the UK would be "wrong".

Rayner said she believed that Mahmood was aware of her position, telling the Times she has "not changed [her] view" since re-entering the cabinet.

Burnham not doing enough to boost growth, says former business secretary

I'm not tempted to call an early election, Burnham says

Before he became prime minister, Burnham said he "understood" where Rayner was coming from on her criticisms of the migrant visa changes, telling reporters in June that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".

Rayner's call for a change of approach has been echoed by York Central Labour MP Rachael Maskell, who also wants a rethink from the home secretary.

She told the Today programme that "technically and morally" what is being proposed represented "the wrong set of values" and would affect "people who have come [to Britain] to serve faithfully and are then told that they have to wait another 10 years" to secure British citizenship.

In recent weeks, trade unions have put pressure on the government to soften its proposals, and a letter to Mahmood jointly signed by dozens of Labour MPs at the start of the year described the plans as "un-British".

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for culture, media and sport, rejected the "un-British" description of the plans.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I don't think they are un-British because I don't think that we have ever had an automatic right to citizenship for most people who come to the UK from overseas."

Nandy said the home secretary was trying to balance respect for people "regardless of who they or where they stand" with the need for "an immigration system that people have confidence in".

Asked if Labour could change its mind on the proposals, she told Today: "We always reserve the right to change our minds but we also will reserve the right to stick to our plans if we think we are getting them right".

The culture secretary said the government will not "change the rules of the game" in a way that unfairly disadvantages migrants who have contributed to the UK.

She said it would "strike the right balance" between treating people "fairly and decently as human beings but making sure there is an asylum and immigration system people can have confidence in."

Nandy's comments are a hint the government is reconsidering. She could have given a full-throated defence of the principle of backdating the changes so they apply to those foreign workers already here.

But she did not. Instead she emphasised the principle of those "contributing" to the UK and treating them fairly.

But if the government does reverse course on applying these changes to those arriving from 2021, the large numbers who came to the UK after that date have a quicker and easier route to settlement. That is a dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK that those parties will be keen to highlight.

The home secretary faced questions about the changes during an appearance at the Home Affairs Committee earlier this week.

Mahmood said she was "very aware that a large group of people who arrived in 2022, absent any change, would qualify in February 2027" for permanent settlement.

She added: "Later this year we will set out the new policy on settlement... as well as any transitional arrangements we might decide to implement."

articles.title: The frat omertà: Whistleblower warns of ‘code of silence’ after Ole Miss deaths, alleged Penn State coke ring
articles.summary: The Ole Miss student death and Penn State cocaine ring allegations echo a deeper crisis in Greek life, says fraternity hazing survivor Andrew Lohse.
articles.body: "You need a code of omertà if you're trying to create an organization that's essentially like a criminal organization," Andrew Lohse said. Lohse was talking about fraternities – the 36-year-old is a fraternity hazing survivor and the author of "Confessions of an Ivy League Frat Boy." As a Dartmouth student, the whistleblower exposed the stomach-turning indoctrination rituals he said he endured inside Sigma Alpha Epsilon. TWO OLE MISS STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS PACKAGED KRATOM IS RECOVERED AT TWO SITES: OFFICIALS When recent headlines came to light regarding the mysterious deaths of two students at Ole Miss – one of whom was in a fraternity – and the alleged frat cocaine distribution ring at Penn State, Lohse said he was immediately reminded of his time as a brother. "For years and years [the last] 10 years, it's like whenever someone dies in a frat, like that's when my phone rings," Lohse told Fox News Digital. OLE MISS NAMES STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS OFFICIAL ADDRESSES POTENTIAL FOR FOUL PLAY One of the Ole Miss students who was found dead this past week, Ryan Strang, was a Phi Delta Theta fraternity brother. He was found at an off-campus home. Authorities found packages of kratom, a commercially available drug that has been derided as "gas station heroin," at both scenes. However, its role in either death was not immediately clear. Phi Delta Theta has not been accused of any wrongdoing. "The loss of two young lives is a profound tragedy," the fraternity said in a statement, in part. "Phi Delta Theta joins the University of Mississippi and the broader Ole Miss community in mourning Robert and Aidan Hamilton and extending our deepest sympathies to their families, friends, chapter brothers, classmates, and all those who knew and loved them. "These losses reinforce the importance of a collective commitment to health, safety, and well-being on college campuses today. We encourage the Phi Delta Theta community to keep the Strang family, the Mississippi Alpha Chapter, and everyone affected by these tragic losses in their thoughts." Dangers like kratom did not exist when Lohse was in school, he said. "There was no kratom, no tranq, no smoking bath salts, no fentanyl. Back then, the cocaine was more or less just cocaine. It wasn't like every time somebody did cocaine they could die." OLE MISS TOXICOLOGY REPORTS EXPECTED SOON AND RESULTS MAY TRIGGER ANTI-FENTANYL LAW, OFFICIAL SAYS At Penn State, prosecutors allege in court documents that pledges were allegedly coerced into cutting and packaging cocaine as part of an alleged organized drug ring led by former Sigma Chi member Agostino Abbatiello. Lohse said, "When I was reading that the pledges were in the background doing that, I thought that was sort of amazing – but in a bad way, but also extremely brazen." PENN STATE COCAINE BUST NETS 14 ARRESTS OVER ALLEGED PLEDGE COKE-CUTTING ‘INDOCTRINATION' RITUALS Fraternity culture made more news this past week in Madison, Wisconsin, where police said they found roughly 30 partially clothed young men packed inside a sweltering basement, covered in food, condiments and other liquids – with several pledges showing signs of being physically assaulted. The Madison Police Department said officers were dispatched to the Alpha Epsilon Pi (AEPi) house on Wednesday night and are investigating the hazing incident, with two people arrested. "AEPi Headquarters takes the allegations involving our Pi Chapter in Madison, Wisconsin, extremely seriously," Jonathan Pierce, the fraternity's chief communications officer, said in a statement. "We will cooperate fully with the authorities investigating this matter." "Hazing is a betrayal of everything our fraternity stands for. There is no place for it in AEPi," he added. "No exceptions. No excuses. We educate our members about their responsibility to ‘Be Your Brothers’ Keeper.’ This is not an optional value." ‘Sad moment’ "It's a sad moment, for society, civilization," Lohse said about some of the recent headlines involving fraternity behavior. "These organizations should be forces of good. Young men need it more than ever. Young men are more adrift than ever, there's no moral leadership." "There's a vacuum in the center of higher education and American society that used to be filled by God, by religion, by the church," he said, adding that it's "totally vacant now." During his time as a brother at Sigma Alpha Epsilon, he said he was forced to "swim in a kiddie pool full of vomit while being urinated on," and "chug" vinegar or milk to the point that he and his fellow pledge brothers "would vomit" in a room covered with tarps. FORMER MICHIGAN HOCKEY PLAYERS ALLEGE COACHES IGNORED YEARS OF ABUSIVE HAZING RITUALS He also said he was forced into a small basement crawl space for a period of time. This was all in addition to constant coerced binge drinking, he said. "We're talking like 10, 15 plus drinks," he said. MIAMI SECRET SERVICE AGENT CHARGED IN NEAR-DEADLY FRATERNITY HAZING, OFFICIALS SAY He said the unwritten "code of silence" or "omertà" contributes to these repeated hazing or drug-related issues within frats. "The original 19th-century concept of the American fraternity is not what exists today," Lohse said. THREE COLLEGE FRATS IN CROSSHAIRS AS HAZING CLAIMS OF BOOZE, BURNS AND HOSPITAL TRIPS SPARK CRACKDOWN: SCHOOL "Essentially, you can look at a modern fraternity like a criminal organization. In most states, the unique behavioral attributes of a fraternity cross into criminal statutes—whether misdemeanor hazing or serious felony drug trafficking. You need a code of silence to protect that." He went on to say, "the organization forces the individual to compromise their own identity for the collective, taking something from its members to ensure the system perpetuates itself over time." GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL Following the hazing incidents during Lohse's time as a student, SAE was suspended from Dartmouth for the last 10 years and re-recognized in August, The Darmouth student-run paper reported. When asked what advice he would offer students considering Greek life at major universities, Lohse stopped short of telling students flatly to avoid fraternities. Instead, Lohse urges young men to calculate the "opportunity cost" before pledging. "Consider that the upside benefit, while maybe not zero, pales in comparison to the downside risk," Lohse said, advising incoming students to reflect on what they truly want out of higher education. SEND US A TIP GOT A TIP? "Think about what you actually want out of college. Who do you really want to be around, and who is actually going to be there to help you? I think you'll find that a fraternity isn't going to provide that." Judson Horras, president and CEO of the North American Interfraternity Conference, told Fox News Digital that "student safety is our members' highest priority. The NIC has adopted enhanced health and safety guidelines and co-led advocacy to pass tougher anti-hazing laws in more than a dozen states, as well as the federal Stop Campus Hazing Act." Regarding the Ole Miss students' deaths, Horras said: "We are heartbroken by the loss of two University of Mississippi students, one of whom was a fraternity member. Our sympathies are with both families and the Ole Miss community. We will continue working with universities and families to keep every student safe." articles.title: ‘No longer trust Washington’: Iran draws red line on peace talks with US
articles.summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Tehran “no longer trust[s] talks with Washington” following what he described as repeated US attacks and
articles.body: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Tehran “no longer trust[s] talks with Washington” following what he described as repeated US attacks and sanctions after negotiations, drawing a clear red line over any renewed diplomatic engagement with the United States.In an interview with Al Jazeera, Pezeshkian said Qatar and Pakistan are currently mediating between Iran and the US and conveying Tehran’s messages to Washington. He said the talks are based on a previous memorandum of understanding signed between the two countries, adding that the “Americans must state their position on it”.Pezeshkian also said Iran would continue to resist pressure from the US and Israel, arguing that those who “thought they could target the Iranian people with sanctions miscalculated”. He accused Washington and Israel of seeking to “prevent Iran from relying on itself”, but said Tehran would instead invest in its people.He said the US and Israel had “dragged” regional countries into war, believing that the Iranian regime “would fall within days”. Instead, he said, Iranians have “stood firm in the face of American and Israeli attacks, and we will continue to stand firm”.His comments come as diplomatic efforts remain stalled over a proposed seven-day ceasefire put forward by Tehran. Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said the proposal would allow the Strait of Hormuz to reopen and nuclear negotiations with Washington to resume if the necessary conditions were met.“If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States,” Araghchi said.“The seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he added.Under the proposal, Washington would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, ease sanctions on Iranian oil exports and observe a ceasefire that includes Lebanon. In return, Tehran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart negotiations over its nuclear programme. Araghchi said the initial measures would take four to five days, with the strait reopening on the sixth day.US President Donald Trump has rejected the proposal, while US officials said he expects American bombing of Iran to resume after the November midterm elections. Trump has publicly said Tehran is seeking a post-midterm deal to dismantle its nuclear programme, while privately remaining sceptical that Iran would meet his demands.Pezeshkian said regional security could instead be achieved through “cooperation among its countries”, arguing that the region does not need a “policeman”.You use AI every day. articles.title: Israel bans Arab parties from election: Who they are, why it matters
articles.summary: Israeli politicians subject to ICC arrest warrants or international sanctions remain eligible to run.
articles.body:
Israel’s Central Elections Committee has voted to bar the country’s two main Arab-majority political lists from next month’s parliamentary election, potentially leaving Palestinian citizens of Israel without their principal representatives in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset.

The committee also voted to disqualify Ofer Cassif , a Jewish politician from the Arab-Jewish Hadash party, and Sami Abu Shehadeh, the leader of the Palestinian nationalist Balad party.

The votes are not the final word on who can run in the October 27 election. The Supreme Court is expected to review the decisions next week and has overturned previous attempts to exclude Arab parties and candidates.

But the committee’s decision has already prompted accusations of double standards, with Palestinian-led parties facing exclusion while parties led by far-right ministers, some of whom have been sanctioned internationally, remaining on the ballot. Here is what the decision means.

The committee voted to disqualify two separate groups. The first is the Joint List, an alliance of Hadash, Balad and Ta’al. The second is Ra’am, also called the United Arab List, which is running on its own. Both rely on support from Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about one-fifth of the country’s population.

This brings together three parties. Hadash is a left-wing party with Jewish and Arab members, Ta’al campaigns primarily for the rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel, and Balad calls for a state with equal rights for all its citizens. They agreed to contest this election on a single list, meaning their candidates would appear together on the ballot.

It is an electoral tactic used to not split votes among parties that are similar ideologically. A list must also win at least 3.25 percent of the national vote to enter the Knesset, so by joining forces, smaller parties combine their votes and reduce the risk that each falls below the threshold – in which case none of them would win seats.

In the current 120-seat Knesset, the Hadash-Ta’al alliance holds five seats. Of the Hadash-Ta’al seats, three belong to Hadash politicians and two to Ta’al. Balad has no seats.

Led by Mansour Abbas , it is running separately. It has been more willing to negotiate with other parties over funding and services for Arab communities. Ra’am joined the broad coalition that governed Israel from 2021 to 2022. The Joint List did not join that government.

In the current Knesset, Ra’am holds five seats.

The decision followed petitions by the right-wing parties, Likud and Otzma Yehudit, which accused the parties and candidates of denying Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state, supporting armed struggle against Israel or inciting racism.

The committee is chaired by a Supreme Court justice, but its voting members represent parties in the outgoing Knesset. Politicians therefore vote on whether rival parties and candidates can contest the election, although the Supreme Court has the final say.

The committee voted 18-5 to bar Ra’am and, in a separate vote, 18-5 to bar the Joint List. It also voted 18-5 to bar Cassif and 31-4 to bar Abu Shehadeh, according to Adalah, the Palestinian legal rights group representing the lists and candidates.

Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara opposed the disqualification of the two lists and Cassif, saying the evidence did not meet the legal threshold. She took a different position on Abu Shehadeh, however. The case against him centres in part on an article he wrote on October 8, 2023, the day after Hamas’s attacks on Israel.

The article was published on the Arab 48 website and referred to the attack as “an important historic event militarily, politically and strategically”.

The attorney general claimed its wording could amount to support for armed struggle.

Abu Shehadeh rejects that reading. He said on X that he opposed armed struggle and supported a “political and civil struggle for peace, justice, and equality”.

Other opposition parties in Israel support the disqualification of Abu Shehadeh. Yair Golan, leader of the opposition Democrats party, said of Abu Shehadeh: “Whoever wants a Jewish-Arab partnership does not speak this way, period,” he said, calling any legitimacy given to armed struggle or harm to civilians “a red line”.

Adalah disputes the case against Abu Shehadeh. It says the article contains no call for violence and argues that the petitions against the Joint List largely rely on old material or positions previously examined by the courts. It plans to challenge the decisions in the Supreme Court.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, remains eligible to run, despite being the subject of an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, and a corruption trial that began in 2020 and remains ongoing. Netanyahu denies the allegations against him.

Cassif, whose disqualification from a previous election was overturned by the Supreme Court in 2019, called Wednesday’s decisions “another nail in the coffin of the remnants of democracy” in Israel. He said he and the Joint List would be in the next Knesset.

Attempts to exclude Arab candidates are not new. Adalah has documented challenges in elections in 2003, 2013, 2015, 2020 and 2022. The Supreme Court has repeatedly reversed committee decisions, but that history offers no guarantee of what it will do this time.

Petitions which sought to disqualify the two far-right ministers in Netanyahu’s cabinet, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit party and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party, were rejected by the election committee.

Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have both advocated the displacement of Palestinians from Gaza and the annexation of the occupied West Bank, and face international sanctions over their actions and rhetoric towards Palestinians.

Attorney General Baharav-Miara, who has repeatedly clashed with Netanyahu’s government, said the bids to bar the far-right parties lacked a legal basis, according to Haaretz. However, for his part, Golan has said he supported disqualifying Ben-Gvir as well.

Netanyahu, meanwhile, remains eligible to run, despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza, and a corruption trial that began in 2020 and remains ongoing. Netanyahu denies the allegations against him.

Human rights advocate Ubai Al-Aboudi condemned the decision. The committee, he told Al Jazeera, has decided “not to bar Israeli politicians, parties or lists that are openly calling for the ethnic cleansing and genocide of Palestinians”.

“It has not even decided to view their statements as extreme.

“This shows that the current Israeli political structure still views Palestinians as a demographic threat, is still vilifying Palestinians.”

About one-fifth of Israel’s population is Palestinian. If the Supreme Court upholds the votes against both Ra’am and the Joint List, voters could still cast ballots for other parties, but neither of the two main Arab-majority lists would be able to contest the election. The court will also decide whether Cassif and Abu Shehadeh can stand.

Al-Aboudi said earlier attempts to bar Arab representatives had been overturned, but this vote went further. “It is the first time that all representation has been barred,” he said, describing it as a sign of “the mentality and extremism of the current Israeli political structure”.

The final decision rests with the Supreme Court. Al-Aboudi said its past rulings offer some grounds for hope, but added that, given the present political atmosphere, it is unclear whether it would overturn “part, all or none” of the committee’s decisions.

articles.title: Iraq loses $60 billion to Iran war as Hormuz squeeze hits oil exports
articles.summary: Iraq is facing a growing economic squeeze as the Iran war disrupts oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, while fuel shortages and rising import costs
articles.body: Iraq is facing a growing economic squeeze as the Iran war disrupts oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, while fuel shortages and rising import costs expose the country's dependence on both oil revenues and imported petroleum products.According to Al Jazeera, the disruption has hit Iraq's oil revenues while pushing up the cost of imported goods, with Iraqi officials warning that the crisis is placing additional pressure on the country's economy. The report also highlights Iraq's struggle to maintain crude exports while meeting domestic demand for refined fuel.Iraq Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said Iraq had lost about $60 billion in oil revenues because of the war, after the country was temporarily unable to export around 90 percent of its oil through its usual Gulf routes. He also described Iraq as facing “extraordinary economic challenges.”The impact is particularly severe because oil revenues account for more than 90 percent of Iraq's federal budget, meaning disruption to crude exports quickly translates into pressure on government finances.Iraq oil minister Basim Mohammed Khudhair told parliament that Iraq's oil exports had fallen to no more than 200,000 barrels per day during the crisis.He said export capacity had subsequently recovered, with Iraq able to move up to 4.254 million barrels per day on September 20, although actual shipments remained dependent on tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.The disruption has also increased the cost of transporting Iraqi crude. During the parliamentary hearing, Khudhair said shipping costs had risen sharply amid the regional conflict, adding further pressure to the revenue Iraq earns from its oil exports.Iraq petrol problemThe disruption has also exposed another weakness in Iraq's oil economy. Despite being one of the world's major crude oil producers, Iraq does not produce enough refined fuel to meet domestic demand and remains dependent on gasoline imports.Iraq's Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudhair told parliament that domestic petroleum-product production stood at around 37 million litres per day, but the country still needed to import at least 5 million litres of gasoline every day to meet demand.Iraq imported an average of 3.907 million litres of gasoline per day in August to help bridge the shortfall, the official said.Iraq looks beyond Hormuz for his oil exportWith exports through the Strait of Hormuz disrupted, Iraq has been turning to its northern route through Kirkuk and Turkey's Ceyhan port to keep crude flowing to international markets.Iraq's Basra Oil Company chief Bassem Abdul Karim said on September 24 that around 250,000 barrels per day of Basra crude was being transported north to Kirkuk for export through Ceyhan, while southern ports were handling about 2.6 million barrels per day.Iraq is also looking at longer-term alternatives. The government has been working to restore and expand pipelines connecting its oilfields to Fishkhabur and Ceyhan, while plans are also being pursued for a western route towards Syria's Mediterranean Baniyas port.You use AI every day. articles.body: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Saturday denied any involvement of Iran in the re-escalated Houthi-Saudi conflict, offering to help resolve the conflict.“What is happening in Yemen is not linked to Iran," Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera, adding that both countries must resolve their conflict through diplomacy.Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of making the Gulf countries fight each other, so that they can control the region's wealth. He said Iran was attacked “from the airspace of Muslim countries”They are “pitting Muslim countries against one another", he said, while highlighting that a "brother" should not fight another.Pezeshkian said that his country will not be a warmonger and has offered to “help resolve the dispute” that escalated in the past few weeks.This statement follows weeks of intensifying violence between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, during which the Iran-backed group has launched barrages of missiles and drones at the kingdom, prompting Saudi airstrikes in response.Between September 10 and 11, Houthi fighters seized the strategically important port city of Mocha. Following this gain, they pushed into the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, taking control of Perim (Mayun) Island before advancing further north to seize the Hanish Islands archipelago.Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces subsequently lost control of the critical Bab el-Mandeb waterway, dealing a significant setback to the kingdom.US rejects seven-day peace proposalPezeshkian also told Al Jazeera that Iran "no longer trusts talks with Washington," citing "repeated attacks and sanctions following every negotiation."According to unnamed US officials cited by The Wall Street Journal, US President Donald Trump has reportedly rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week, keeping the possibility of further strikes open.Iran's military has cautioned that all US deployment centres and interests in the region will become targets if Washington "makes a mistake" against the country, according to the semi-official Mehr news agency.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Not talking on behalf of EC': Union minister says 'no proof' of EC-SIR row, slams opposition
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister Prahlad Joshi on Saturday hit out at the opposition over its protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar amid the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Prahlad Joshi on Saturday hit out at the opposition over its protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar amid the ongoing controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, saying there was no “concrete proof” to support the allegations being raised against the Election Commission.Reacting to the opposition's claims, Joshi said the protest was an expression of the “pain” caused by its electoral defeat. He said the SIR issue was being used to voice that distress.“The pain in their hearts caused by their defeat... they are trying to express that distress through the SIR issue,” Joshi said.His remarks came in response to questions about a report published by The Indian Express, which cited concerns allegedly raised within the Election Commission over the SIR exercise. The report claimed that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised 14 written dissents or objections over a 10-month period.The reports led the opposition to seek action against CEC Gyanesh Kumar and demand a halt to the SIR, while the ECI said internal notes, queries and differences of view are part of its functioning and maintained that all final decisions on the exercise were unanimous.Joshi said that even if the report was taken into consideration, it did not amount to conclusive evidence of wrongdoing.“Whatever has appeared in The Indian Express... if you even believe that, I am not saying they have no right, but I am also saying that it is not concrete proof for that. It is not at all concrete proof,” he said.Joshi also disputed the opposition's suggestion that decisions related to the SIR were taken unilaterally. Referring to the Election Commission's own press release, he said decisions of the poll panel had been unanimous.“And whatever has been written in The Indian Express, even that never states that a unilateral decision was taken. All the decisions—all, I am not saying almost—all the decisions of the Election Commission have been taken unanimously,” Joshi said.The Union minister, however, clarified that he was not speaking on behalf of the poll panel.“I am not talking on behalf of the Election Commission, but I am speaking based on the press release issued by the Election Commission,” Joshi said.The opposition has been protesting against CEC Gyanesh Kumar over the SIR exercise and has raised questions about the manner in which the electoral-roll revision is being conducted.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Hum Auratein Azaad Hain’: DU students hold march
articles.summary: DU women students marched from Kamala Nehru College after alleged Aastha Kunj Park rape, demanding safer public spaces, lighting, transport and accountability.
articles.body: New Delhi: Women students from several Delhi University colleges took out a march Friday on the issue of safety after the alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl at Aastha Kunj Park.Beginning at the gate of Kamala Nehru College, the march carried the message “Hum Auratein Azaad Hain” (we, the women, are free) and was open to women and gender minorities. According to a student, the march started around 3:30 pm and went on till late in the evening.The students called for better street lighting and easier access to public transport, saying women should be able to travel to college or work and use public spaces without fear. They also opposed restrictions on women’s movement after dark, arguing that such curbs place the burden of safety on women themselves. Instead, they urged authorities to address unsafe conditions in public spaces and ensure accountability for violence against women.They also argued that surveillance and restrictions should not be treated as substitutes for wider safety measures. A student said consultations on a “Charter of Demands for Delhi Citizens” would be held on Siri Fort Road, near Gargi College and Kamala Nehru College, after the march.At North Campus, the Delhi University unit of Students’ Federation of India held a separate march from Arts Faculty. Held under the slogan “Make Delhi Safe Again”, the protest raised concerns about crimes against women and the safety of women students in and around university campuses.Meanwhile, LSR Students’ Union said it had received regular updates on increased patrolling around the college, including in National Park and Vikram Vihar, as well as Pink Squad patrols. It said personnel stationed at Pink Booth and the college’s back gate were being monitored and briefed. Work was also under way to improve street lighting on the road behind the college and address specific spots students had flagged as unsafe, according to the union.The union said it would continue following up on students’ concerns and check whether the measures were visible and effective on the ground. It asked students to report what had improved, what remained unchanged and whether they felt safer travelling to and from college.Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad, Delhi also staged a demonstration outside the Delhi Police headquarters over growing concerns regarding the safety of women and girl students in the capital. ABVP activists expressed serious concern over incidents involving the students in various parts of Delhi and around university campuses. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami participated in the BJP's anti-drug campaign, which is being seen as the party's outreach effort
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami participated in the BJP's anti-drug campaign, which is being seen as the party's outreach effort ahead of next year's state elections. Dhami arrived in Mukerian in Punjab's Hoshiarpur Rural area and participated in a roadshow, riding on a tractor. A large crowd gathered to welcome CM Dhami, with a massive public turnout witnessed during the roadshow. He also addressed a large public gathering in Mukerian.Dhami also campaigned in Dasuya and said the BJP was committed to making Punjab drug-free, asserting that the campaign against drug abuse would be taken to every household and individual in the state.Speaking during his visit to Dasuya, Dhami said, "I have come with PM Modi's message and a resolve to make Punjab drug-free. Our party is running a campaign against drugs and striving to reach every household and every individual."Targeting the Aam Aadmi Party government in Punjab, Dhami said, "The AAP government had promised to make Punjab a drug-free state within three months, but the situation today is unfortunate; those who raise their voices against drugs are harassed and even driven to suicide."He further said, "Under PM Modi's leadership, all pledges have been fulfilled-be it the abrogation of Article 370 or the elimination of terrorism and Naxalism. Similarly, drug abuse will be eradicated from Punjab as well."Dhami also said that Union home minister Amit Shah's visit would strengthen the ongoing campaign."The visit of Union home minister Amit Shah will give momentum to our campaign," he said.The remarks come as the BJP is conducting its 'Nasha Mukt Punjab Yatra', a 13-day anti-drug campaign launched on September 18. Four simultaneous yatras are covering nearly 4,000 km across all 117 Assembly constituencies before culminating in Jalandhar on September 30. Amit Shah is scheduled to address the concluding programme in Jalandhar.The Centre has also outlined a roadmap to make India drug-free by 2029, with the government focusing on coordination among central and state agencies, dismantling drug networks, and prevention and awareness programmes.Punjab's ruling AAP has separately been running its 'Yudh Nashean Virudh' campaign, which includes action against drug networks, prevention initiatives, community participation and treatment for people affected by addiction.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Hot and dry weather could lead to butterfly 'population crash'
articles.summary: More than 77,000 butterflies were recorded in Devon while 47,000 were spotted in Cornwall this July.
articles.body:
Butterfly and day-flying moth numbers recorded across Devon and Cornwall this summer have been "very good" - but experts fear prolonged hot and dry weather could lead to a decline.

Nearly 5,000 people took part in the Butterfly Conservation's 2026 big butterfly count in Devon, recording 77,151 insects during the three-week count. It said nearly 3,000 people took part in Cornwall, spotting 47,712.

Head of science at the conservation, professor Richard Fox, said adult butterflies loved hot weather, but warned we could be on course "for a population crash".

"The extreme droughts in 1976 and 1995 had severe impacts on butterfly populations, with some species never fully recovering," he said.

The charity said strong butterfly numbers was "likely" down to favourable conditions for caterpillars in spring, followed by the hot, sunny weather enjoyed by adult butterflies during the summer months.

However, it said previous drought conditions across much of the UK may have caused food plants used by caterpillars to wither before they had finished feeding. The charity fears the full impact may not become clear until next year.

Fox said many species were already under pressure, with 80% of the UK's butterfly populations having declined since the 1970s.

"So many are already struggling for survival, without these extreme weather pressures," Fox said.

He added: "With increasingly hot, dry summers and droughts predicted to become more and more frequent due to climate breakdown, degraded habitats and already depleted butterfly populations, some species may be pushed further and faster towards extinction, which is a very sombre thought.

"They are, quite simply, less resilient to these events, which means we could be looking at very difficult years ahead."

The charity is urging people to help wildlife recover by planting more trees and shrubs, installing water butts to store rainwater and leaving areas of grass uncut.

The Gatekeeper was the most commonly spotted butterfly in Devon and Cornwall.

The Meadow Brown took the second spot in Devon, followed by the Red Admiral. In Cornwall, the Red Admiral took second spot, followed by the Painted Lady.

Butterfly Conservation said the Painted Lady was one of the standout species with 6,955 recorded in Devon and 6,033 in Cornwall. The migratory butterfly enjoyed a strong year nationally.

Painted Ladies undertake one of the world's most remarkable insect migrations, travelling from Africa to the UK over several generations, crossing the Sahara Desert and Mediterranean Sea.
